entry.content:
Yes, we’re talking to you. Plus, Steve Aoki’s two-hour job search and the art of collecting weird things.

Internet Microdoses

Nike is taking over Formula 1. Starting in 2027, the swoosh replaces Puma as F1's official uniform supplier, alongside a new partnership with the all-female F1 Academy. Finally, a brand befitting the staff who get out there and just do it. (And the drivers who don’t. Looking at you, Lance Stroll.) 

See the new F1 fits →

Google wants to give you main character syndrome. The company filed a patent application for a 24/7 AI-generated TV channel starring you. Your watch history would shape the plot. What Google knows about you would determine which ads run during the breaks. Finally, a show your friends have a legitimate excuse not to watch.

See who's been cast as you →

SSENSE is under fire for allegedly using AI to alter product photos. The retailer reportedly laid off most of its photo and makeup team this summer. Designers Reese Cooper and Gerrit Jacob called out the warped zippers and smeared prints. The sale section, though, is still very much real. 

See the pants fused to shoes →

Steve Aoki quit his LinkedIn job search after two hours. The DJ set up a profile to look for a "real job" after years of throwing sheet cakes at EDM audiences. He took an "intentional micro-sabbatical" after writing one cover letter. Still, that’s more than most people are doing on LinkedIn. 

What throwing cake taught him about B2B sales →

Hailey Bieber says her billion-dollar brand is built on "optimistical delusion." Speaking at the New York Times DealBook Summit, the Rhode founder shared her approach to building her brand while wearing a 1998 Yohji Yamamoto jacket identical to one famously worn by Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy.

How to sell lip balm for a billion dollars →

For the person who said “just bring yourself.” You’ll probably hear that more than once between now and New Year’s. If showing up empty-handed feels like taking your host a little too literally, we put together a few things we’d bring to dinner. You can take the credit.

entry.title: Simi Table Lamp
entry.summary: Three pieces of brushed aluminum slot together to make a miniature solar eclipse for your side table.
entry.content:
Three pieces of brushed aluminum slot together to make a miniature solar eclipse for your side table.

HueGah Home's Simi Table Lamp is built from three flat pieces of brushed aluminum slotted together: a circular reflector disc behind an arched front shield that hides the bulb. Instead of shining light directly into the room, the curved front panel bounces a warm halo onto the metal circle behind it. It comes in two sizes and looks a bit like a miniature solar eclipse sitting on a side table.

HueGah Home started in Los Angeles in 2022, founded by Parsons-trained interior designer Bailey Elaine. Named after the Danish word for coziness, the studio pulls from Art Deco and mid-century design to make smaller objects that change the mood of a room. Raw aluminum usually feels cold and industrial, so using it to diffuse warm light is a welcome trick.

The small lamp costs $200 (regularly $285).

entry.title: Naomi Sharon
entry.summary: On frosted glass buildings, Céline Dion on repeat, and giving Still Awake one side for a night in and another for a night out.
entry.content:
On frosted glass buildings, Céline Dion on repeat, and giving Still Awake one side for a night in and another for a night out.

Naomi Sharon started out in musical theater before becoming the first woman signed to Drake's OVO Sound. Born in Rotterdam and now based in Los Angeles, the Dutch-Caribbean singer blends R&B, electronic music, and soul. She followed her 2023 debut, Obsidian, with No Sleep In Paradise earlier this year. This month, she expanded it into Still Awake, rearranging the entire tracklist into two sides: one for nights in, the other for nights out. Here, Naomi talks about frosted glass buildings, listening to Céline Dion on repeat, and investing in herself.

Tell us more about what you’ve been working on recently.

No Sleep In Paradise has always been a reflection of where I was emotionally and creatively at the time. Throughout the process, I allowed myself to explore different sounds without feeling the need to fit into one particular genre.

With Still Awake, I wanted to expand on that world rather than just add a few extra songs. We actually rearranged the entire tracklist to integrate the newer sound and give the album a different flow.

That’s where the idea of Side A and Side B came from. One for a night in and one for a night out. Both sides carry a different energy, but they still belong to the same world. I liked the idea of giving people two different ways to experience the album, depending on their mood.

Can you tell us more about your creative process?

I like to get inspired by life experiences.

What's your hot take?

Spiritual psychosis was a real thing during COVID.

Three places you’ve felt inspired by.

Islands, Los Angeles, buildings with frosted glass.

What do you listen to on repeat?

Céline Dion (everything).

What are the most worthwhile investments you’ve made?

In myself, in my skincare routine, in my relationships, in my career, in my beauty.

What is an unusual habit or an absurd thing that you love?

You can wake me up for a fuet sausage.

Who is your forever inspo?

Céline Dion and Whitney Houston, both insane performers and storytellers.

Write us a fortune cookie message.

This too will pass.

entry.title: A Collection of Oddities
entry.summary: From cabinets of curiosities to camera rolls, the odd things we collect and what happens when we put them side by side.
entry.content:
From cabinets of curiosities to camera rolls, the odd things we collect and what happens when we put them side by side.

A lot of us spend a significant amount of time saving inspiring art, runway looks, weird chairs, and random scans to a drive somewhere, a Cosmos collection, or our camera rolls. Last year at the Museum at FIT in New York, a dress by Mary Katrantzou was covered in beaded butterflies and seashells, while earrings were displayed inside glass science jars.

It looked like a "cabinet of curiosities," a private room rich Europeans used to fill with rare stuff in the 1600s to show off how much of the world they knew.

Walk into one of those rooms, and you could see a shell from one ocean and a kayak from another without taking a step. Collectors used ceiling hooks, special drawers, and gold stands to put things side by side that no one there had ever seen together.

Centuries before we started saving images to collections, people were already building little worlds out of the things that fascinated them.

TikTok-style videos are getting their own film fest. Microdramas are series made for phones, told in episodes of one to three minutes. At October's Alza Festival in New York, each one played in a thin strip with five feet of black on either side. The only downside is you can’t scroll past.

You can now bet on the art world. Kalshi, the prediction market, has teamed up with Artnet so users can trade yes-or-no contracts on November's big New York sales. Miami Art Week is next. Finally, you can lose money on a masterpiece without buying it.

Going once, going twice →

Jensen Huang’s viral fit was an AI fantasy. After the former NVIDIA CEO admitted to an affair with a Chinese executive reportedly suspected of spying, a photo of him in a studded Saint Laurent jacket went viral. It was AI, edited onto a June picture of him in Dior. He’s due before Congress on December 1, which means there’s still time for him to buy one.

Check the stitching →

Maybe. Maybelline. Went. Too. Far. The brand’s new Miley Cyrus campaign gives its familiar slogan a punctuation makeover: “Maybe. We’re born with it. Maybe. It’s Maybelline.” The brand’s president says the old line was “giving ambiguity.” The new one’s giving hiccups.

Read between the periods →

GTA VI’s research involved clubbing and cops. In 2015, Rockstar developers stayed out in Miami clubs until 4 a.m. and rode along with South Beach cops. Almost 5,000 people then built Vice City, down to the insides of the fridges. Florida Man is getting a glow-up.

Take the scenic route →

Damienciaga is here. For the 25th birthday of Balenciaga's Le City bag, shock artist Damien Hirst covered it in his spots, butterflies and pill stickers. The designs spill onto sneakers and bomber jackets too. Hirst once preserved a shark in formaldehyde. Now he's preserving the 2000s.

entry.content:
Ancient architecture meets the post-dinner sweet tooth in a stainless steel ice cream cup and column-inspired spoon.

Service Projects' Ice Cream Cup 02 is shaped like an hourglass: a wide, shallow cone of brushed stainless steel balanced on a smaller one. Fine ridges circle both halves and catch the light like the grooves of a record. The matching Canteen teaspoon has a handle fluted like a Greek column. Both were designed by Laura Bilde, who was named upcoming designer of the year at the Danish Design Awards in 2016.

Service Projects started in New York in 2022 with the idea of bringing restaurant-kitchen steel home, and it now works out of Copenhagen. The brand says the line was inspired by ancient architecture, a surprisingly sophisticated setting for a scoop of ice cream. Sure, we may put away childish things, but the post-meal sweet tooth is eternal.

Four cups cost $119, and four spoons are $70.

entry.title: Aliens Exist
entry.summary: From Panton’s psychedelic interiors to Giger’s skeletal bar, why design is looking a little more alien.
entry.content:
From Panton’s psychedelic interiors to Giger’s skeletal bar, why design is looking a little more alien.

For most of the 2010s, everything looked like it came out of the same mood board: a tidy sans-serif logo, millennial pink, a beige couch. Suddenly, searches for “aliencore” are up 80%, and the stuff in our feeds suggests the truth is out there. Glowing green glass lamps, spiky enamel rings, wraparound sunglasses with a warped logo.

In 1970, the chemical company Bayer rented a boat during the Cologne furniture fair and hired the Danish designer Verner Panton to turn it into a showroom. He built Fantasy Landscape, a room of curving, organic shapes in saturated color. It looked like the inside of another planet, and it was there to sell synthetic materials.

Not all aliens want the same thing. Some want to survive. Others want to sell plastic. But most of them are just trying to find a way home.

entry.title: Tal Silberstein
entry.summary: On starting with fabric, writing by hand, and the Alice Coltrane record that’s watched over the shop since day one.
entry.content:
On starting with fabric, writing by hand, and the Alice Coltrane record that’s watched over the shop since day one.

Before Colbo, Tal Silberstein ran a little record shop that also sold magazines, ceramics, scents and, eventually, clothes he made himself. From DJing, throwing events and working with designers, he learned how a space can bring people together. Colbo, which means "everything in it", opened on the Lower East Side in 2021. Today there's the clothing shop on Orchard, a wine bar called Next Door on Allen, a spot at ESTNATION in Tokyo and an LA pop-up through the end of the year. People come for a shirt and stay for a glass of wine. Here, he talks about the label’s five-year anniversary, why the best pieces start with the fabric, and the Alice Coltrane record that's watched over the counter since day one.

What’s been going on at Colbo recently?

We're celebrating five years of Colbo and one year of Next Door, our wine bar, November 19–22. It'll be a long weekend of music, food, friends and a holiday capsule we made for the anniversary.

We've also extended our LA pop-up on N Virgil, next to our good friends at Courage Bagels, through the end of the year! It's been exciting to see how Colbo feels in another city and to get to know the community there.

We also just released Sirah, a new silhouette we developed with our longtime collaborator Sperry.

And we just wrapped a collab with Artforum for their inaugural Art Week: a small capsule that's available in store, online, in LA and at the New Museum, plus a site-specific exhibition across both our NY spaces.

So, there's a lot happening at once, as usual! + more to come ;)

Tell us your favorite products from your recent collection

The Chinos in Soft Dark Brown. One of my favorite pairs of pants. They're loose and easy, in an Italian linen and wool blend that we also used for a matching blazer. I love them as a suit or just worn casually.

The Suit Overcoat. It's been my everyday winter coat for the last few years, and this season we made it in a Tumble Greige. The washed wool has that familiar, already-worn feeling I love. It's tailored and oversized at the same time, so there's room to wear it over everything.

The Mel Jacket. It's a relatively new shape for us, with some really cool flaps, vents and athletic details, like the elastic cuff and thumb hole, but made in the most unique fabrics we could source. Kind of our take on tech.

Shop Colbo’s fall collection →

Tell us about the history of Colbo. What inspired you then vs. now? Give us some brand lore!

Colbo means "everything in it", and that's what it is. Everything I've experienced so far and feel the urge to share: music, clothes, hospitality, community and art, all in one place.

After traveling the world and studying art in New York, in 2015 I opened a little record shop called BVRLY, with magazines, ceramics, scents and eventually clothes I started making. At the same time I was working with Hed Mayner, DJing and throwing events. Later, being part of Public Records in Brooklyn showed me how far that idea could go.

Colbo came out of all of that in 2021, on the Lower East Side. Now there's the shop on Orchard, Next Door on Allen, our space at ESTNATION in Tokyo, and a team that believes in it as much as I do and keeps pushing forward!

We're building a world more than a brand. It's more about a lifestyle, a feeling, a presence, a way of being. People come in for a shirt, stay for a glass of wine and a record, and come back because it feels like theirs. A little bit of a cult, in the best way.

Tell us more about your creative process.

I usually start with fabric. I'll find a texture, color or treatment that interests me and start thinking about what it could become. Sometimes it fits into a shape we've been working on; sometimes it calls for something completely new, and sometimes it goes the other way and a shape sends me looking for the right fabric.

It's always very intuitive and physical. I need to touch things, try them on and see how they move. I might love each piece on its own, but the feeling comes from what I put next to it. I think about clothes, music and spaces in a similar way.

Ideas can come from anywhere. Traveling, meeting people, going to dinner, just things that happen over the course of a day. I'm also really drawn to the past, to vintage clothes and older ways of living and spending time. Nature and spirituality are always in there too. I like seeing how those feelings come through in the clothes and spaces we're making now.

Which three places have inspired you?

India, where I spent over a year traveling when I was young. That time opened up a lot for me around spirituality, music, energy and different ways of living and dressing.

Milan. To me it's the coolest, most unassuming city. Naturally stylish and chic, the best food and amazing people. All of Italy, really. Super inspiring, from the culture and fashion to the aesthetics, nature, lifestyle and beyond.

The desert. You can probably see it in my color palette, lol, but it's also where I feel deeply calm. There's so much space, tonality, structure and silence. It feels like a place for the spirit, somewhere I can meditate, reconnect and get inspired.

What do you listen to on repeat?

Alice Coltrane is someone I always return to. Her music has this deep, meditative quality that's been part of my life and Colbo from the beginning. We've had one of her records above the counter since day one, just watching over the space. Otherwise, my listening goes in a lot of directions, from jazz and ambient/electronic to soul, reggae, post-punk and beyond.

What’s a daily ritual that shapes the way you work?

Every morning I write out all my to-dos with a pencil on paper, across everything I’m working on. I redo the list the same way every day. It’s the only way I can keep track of everything. I think writing things by hand helps them stick in memory and become ingrained in the brain.

I’ve also used my own handwriting in a lot of Colbo’s graphics over the years, and I still do. It’s something I’ve used in other projects in the past too.

Who is your forever inspo?

Giorgio Armani. There's something so beautiful about clothes that have that much thought behind them and still feel completely relaxed on a person. I keep coming back to his proportions, fabrics and colors, and to the ideas and campaigns that built the brand over the years.

The New York Times wants Letterboxd. The Times Company is in exclusive talks to buy the app, where 30 million movie buffs log and review what they watch, for roughly $330 million. Now your one-line review of You Can See Everything could belong to the paper of record.

Rate this deal →

Kim Kardashian is sorry for her advent calendar. SKIMS charged $148 for 12 doors of hair ties, scrunchies, bobby pins and something called a "bra elastic headband." After a TikTok unboxing got tens of millions of views, SKIMS emailed buyers to say "we fell short this time."

Was this another marketing stunt? →

The fastest way out of Google's office is a slide. Carsten Höller installed four spiral slides, the tallest about 125 feet, at Antara, an open-air mall in Polanco, Mexico City. Riders can start from the Google offices, the Rosewood Hotel or the restaurants, and every slide ends at the same exit. Finally, a legitimate way to escape the all-hands.

Take the fast way down →

The Cybertruck is driving into the sunset. Slowly. Elon Musk is winding down production due to low sales. He once claimed more than a million reservations, but fewer than 50,000 trucks had sold by March last year. To be fair, its "unbreakable" windows did break twice when it was first unveiled.

Rest in pieces →

Martine Rose's plot twist comes with Balenciaga. In March, the company that owned most of her brand overruled her, turned down her bid to buy it back, then sold it. On November 16, she becomes the first woman to run Balenciaga in its 109 years. She started as Demna's consultant in 2015. Now she's the boss.

The design fair just wrapped its third edition in a former Upper East Side cinema, with more than 110 exhibitors from 27 countries and a section staged as office cubicles. Now it's turning Club Collectible into events that run all year. Like a return-to-office mandate, but you'll want to go.

entry.title: Marcus Milione
entry.summary: Minted New York’s founder on romanticizing quitting, ’90s trance, and finding inspiration in the New York City skyline.
entry.content:
Minted New York’s founder on romanticizing quitting, ’90s trance, and finding inspiration in the New York City skyline.

Marcus Milione started Minted New York on his lunch breaks while working in commercial real estate debt. It began on TikTok, where he’d post three videos a day about fashion and fitness, usually wearing jewelry he'd made himself. Viewers wanted the jewelry, so he started selling it. Today, Minted New York has grown into a brand spanning performance running apparel, menswear, and jewelry, while also venturing into documentary filmmaking. They just released their first documentary: a 50-minute film about Olympic medalist Grant Fisher. Here, Marcus talks about why we've romanticized quitting, the ’90s trance he has on repeat, and why the New York City skyline continues to inspire him.

Shop Minted New York’s Fall Performance Running collection →

What's your hot take?

I think we've romanticized quitting things that are difficult. There's this idea online that if something isn't making you happy, you should walk away from it. Obviously, there are situations where that's the right decision, but I think we've lost some appreciation for sticking with things when they're genuinely hard.

Three places you’ve felt inspired by.

Anytime I drive back into NYC at night and can see the skyline in the distance. You look out the window and realize that human beings, through sheer willpower, built all of this out of nothing. Early mornings in Central Park. Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris.

What do you listen to on repeat?

Right now? ’90s trance classics (“Netherworld” by LSG, “Seven Days” by BBE, etc.), but it’s always changing. Tomorrow it might be “45” by Shinedown. Depends on my mood that day.

What are the most worthwhile investments you’ve made?

Running, a Wüsthof chef’s knife, regular dental checkups and cleanings, and Eight Sleep.

Can you tell us more about your creative process?

I tend to be an overthinker, and because of that, I can sometimes find myself focusing too much on the edge cases, the things that could go wrong, or the reasons why an idea might not work before I've even given it a chance.

As I've become less involved in the day-to-day product design (shout-out to Clay, Shawn, etc.) and more focused on the bigger, less tangible world of brand building and creative direction, I've found that a lot of my thinking happens while I'm running. I don't run with music, so I spend a lot of time alone with my thoughts.

Some days, ideas come naturally, and I can work through something that's been on my mind for weeks without much effort. Other days, it feels like I'm banging my head against a brick wall, turning the same idea over and over without getting anywhere.

I think one of the things I've learned is that you can't really force creativity, but you can create the conditions for it to happen. There's value in continuing to show up, giving yourself the space to think, and trusting that the work you're putting in will eventually lead somewhere.

What is an unusual habit, or an absurd thing, that you love?

I'm sure it doesn't count as unusual, but I love going to sleep early. There's nothing like getting under the covers after being spent from a long day and knowing I can turn off my brain until my eyes open in the morning.

Who is your forever inspo?

How do I narrow it down to one? I find myself interested in too many things to look at life through one lens. I'm a builder at heart, and I've always admired people that build great, enduring things. I have a tremendous amount of respect for world-building, particularly the ability to take a single idea and turn it into something that extends far beyond a physical product. People like Ralph Lauren, Jim Jannard, and Melanie Perkins all come to mind, each for different reasons.

Write us a fortune cookie message.

Life is the longest game you'll ever play. Learn to love the long game.

Wired earbuds get blown up into a dog leash, with 10% of proceeds helping rescue dogs in LA.

This dog leash doubles as a giant novelty pair of white earbuds, 3D-printed and attached to a 70-inch white leather leash. It’s a collaboration between the dog accessories brand Girl and a Stray Dog and Beata Rydbacken, a Stockholm designer best known for hair clips about the size of your forearm. She prints them, then puts every one together by hand. She also made the hat out of blonde hair that Rosalía wore on tour.

Rydbacken has always been obsessed with scale. She told Vogue Scandinavia that as a kid, she used to cry because she wanted to be 10 centimeters tall. Wired earbuds have been making a comeback because they’re so unassuming, which doesn’t really work when they’re blown up this big. Still, with big ’phones comes big responsibility, and 10% of proceeds go to Hot Girls Care Foundation, which rescues high-risk dogs from overcrowded LA shelters.

entry.title: Showing your work
entry.summary: As AI makes ads easier to produce, brands are showing how much work went into making theirs by hand.
entry.content:
As AI makes ads easier to produce, brands are showing how much work went into making theirs by hand.

For the last two years, Coca-Cola has used AI to remake its 1995 holiday ad, the one with the glowing red trucks. Both times, people hated it.

Everyone else seems to be doing the opposite: making painstaking ads by hand and making sure everyone knows it. Levi's crew spent four hours filming every second of its stop-motion yeti. Prada put "Animated by Hand" right under the title of its holiday film, then made a second film about the animators themselves.

For all the talk of prompts replacing animators, handmade films are having a major moment.

Internet Microdoses

New York to London in 3.5 hours? Not so fast. Boom Supersonic promised a jet that could fly overseas in half the current time. Passengers were expected in the air by 2029, but United's CEO says that's not happening. The airline agreed to conditionally buy 15 jets, but Boom hasn't completed a single prototype of the passenger jet.

Please remain seated →

Three of the world's biggest modern art museums are teaming up. MoMA in New York, the Centre Pompidou in Paris and M+ in Hong Kong will put on exhibitions together and share their collections. Together they attract 10 million visitors a year: think of it as the art world's biggest group project.

Three cities, one alliance →

Could the right apartment cure your loneliness? Frank Lloyd Wright warned that cities were making us feel isolated nearly 100 years ago. Now, architects are rethinking how we live together. Some have designed building has shared balconies, communal dining rooms, and have cheaper rent for young folks who help their older neighbors. Maybe the problem really does start at home.

Meet the neighbors →

Part of London's Oxford Street just banned cars. On October 26, more than half a mile of the tourist destination closed to cars, buses, taxis and bikes, 10 years after the mayor first promised it. Finally, window-shopping without having to dodge a double-decker.

Take a walk →

Someone moved a 1950s house to the other end of France. Designed by Claude Prouvé using his father Jean's construction system, the house was built with factory-made parts. When it was about to be torn down, a collector took it apart and rebuilt it among olive trees in the south. Flat-pack furniture could never.

Book a stay →

A Kandinsky painting has gone up nearly 100,000% in value. In 1964, the Guggenheim was making space and sold Betonte Ecken to a New York dealer for just $62,000. On November 17, Christie’s expects that exact canvas to fetch between $60 million and $80 million. This is why you should never throw anything out.

entry.title: Atiba Jefferson
entry.summary: Your favorite skater’s favorite photographer talks Virgil Abloh, mango with almonds, and the case for being nice.
entry.content:
Your favorite skater’s favorite photographer talks Virgil Abloh, mango with almonds, and the case for being nice.

Atiba Jefferson found his place in skateboarding by photographing the people he'd been skating with for years. More than 30 years later, he's your favorite skater's favorite photographer. He's a staff photographer for Thrasher, but his influence spreads wider than the skate scene. He's photographed the Lakers and hangs out with everyone from Turnstile to Tim Robinson. A true alternative icon, he just dropped his second collection with Vans. Here, he shares his case for being nice, why Virgil Abloh inspires him, and his love of mango with almonds.

Can you tell us more about your creative process?

As a photographer, I’m inspired as soon as I open my eyes. I can’t turn off wanting to take photos.

What’s your hot take?

There is no excuse for people to be mean or rude.

Three places you’ve felt inspired by.

Any skate spot, basketball game or concert that I go to.

What do you listen to on repeat?

Turnstile.

What are the most worthwhile investments you’ve made?

Hard work is the best payoff, but also Saint Archer, a beer company I invested in.

What is an unusual habit, or an absurd thing, that you love?

I like the combo of mango and almonds.

Who is your forever inspo?

Virgil Abloh is a huge inspiration to me; he broke every rule.

entry.title: The Corner 022
entry.summary: After years in front of the camera, a model decides how much of his face to show.
entry.content:
After years in front of the camera, a model decides how much of his face to show.

Sang Woo Kim's The Corner 022 (2026) is a self-portrait cropped so close that only half his face fits: one eye, the side of his nose, half his mouth and an ear. He painted the skin in oil and acrylic, mixing ochre, orange and tan with a little green and gray. Kim was born in Seoul in 1994 and moved to Britain as a child. He lives in London, and in May his work was shown in Venice during the Biennale.

Growing up, he was one of very few Asian kids in his school and faced racial discrimination, with bullies focusing on the shape of his eyes. Later, working as a model, he saw the fashion industry fetishize the same feature. Now, he’s reclaiming his features as the focus of his own work. In a 2024 artist statement, he made his intentions clear: “As I become more of myself – the artist – the more I intend to reveal of my face, body, autonomy.”

entry.title: Everything is hardcore
entry.summary: How the hoodies, work pants, and sneakers worn in mosh pits and on skate ramps became an everyday uniform.
entry.content:
How the hoodies, work pants, and sneakers worn in mosh pits and on skate ramps became an everyday uniform.

A gray Champion hoodie, Adidas track pants or Dickies workwear, Vans or a pair of Jordans, and a varsity jacket for when it's cold out. That’s the default outfit you throw on to run errands, do laundry, or lie around your living room all Sunday.

But forty years ago, that look was also a uniform for the misfits. In the mid-'80s, a scene of New York hardcore kids showed up to shows dressed for gym class, starting a movement that would be known as youth crew. In California, pro skaters were throwing themselves down ramps in similar fits.

For most of us, this outfit feels like a nice neutral when we don't want to overthink. But the true heads in our midst know the hardcore and skate history stitched into it.

entry.title: Jackie
entry.summary: A towering beaded jack-o’-lantern with precious stones forming the rot inside.
entry.content:
A towering beaded jack-o’-lantern with precious stones forming the rot inside.

Kathleen Ryan's Jackie (2021) is a jack-o'-lantern with its lid tipped over on the floor beside it. The skin is studded with tens of thousands of acrylic beads. The rot inside is lapis, malachite, amethyst, and agate, pinned on by hand. She usually saves the cheap beads for the fresh parts and the real stones for the decay, so the moldiest bit is worth the most. It stands over 5 feet tall.

Ryan was born in Santa Monica in 1984 and minored in archaeology. Before grad school, she coordinated Jeff Koons's plastics projects at the fabricator Carlson & Co. Her Bad Fruit series started in 2018 with beaded plastic fruit she found in thrift stores. Jackie is now in the Nasher Sculpture Center's collection in Dallas. Its grin gives a view of the rot inside.

entry.title: Hair lines
entry.summary: From towering ship hairstyles to bleached headphones, a history of wearing your identity in your hair.
entry.content:
From towering ship hairstyles to bleached headphones, a history of wearing your identity in your hair.

April Harper Grey is best known as underscores, one of the biggest names in hyperpop, a genre of experimental electronic pop music. The 26-year-old singer and producer released her third album, U, in March, and this fall she's opening for Charli XCX in arenas. You can recognize her by her hair: dark, with the outline of a pair of headphones bleached into it. Her fans are recreating the design on their own heads.

People have worn symbols in their hair to show what they believe in or who they admire for centuries. In 1778, after a French frigate (a warship) fought a British ship, women at the French court in Versailles built model ships into hairstyles up to two feet high.

Since then, people have dyed, shaved, and bleached everything from AIDS ribbons to Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper into their hair.

entry.title: Adriana Roslin
entry.summary: A Madrid-born photographer and creative director creating minimal, architectural images shaped by light.
entry.content:
A Madrid-born photographer and creative director creating minimal, architectural images shaped by light.

Adriana Roslin starts every shoot by finding the right light. The Madrid-born creative director and photographer chooses locations for how light falls across their surfaces. Her minimal, almost architectural images have appeared in Vogue Spain and GQ Spain. Her clients include Loewe, Adidas, and Spotify. Right now, she's juggling a shoe campaign, a project for the Spanish airline Iberia, and a documentary. Here, Adriana shares her case against Instagram, the best investments she's made, and the airport pat-down videos that give her ASMR.

What's your hot take?

Instagram has become this major dystopian TV screen that feeds our insecurities, our anger, and our despair. We are constantly forced to witness the misuse of power by influencers and celebrities who are, whether we like it or not, a big pillar of contemporary “culture.” They are there, and companies and fans continue to give them massive platforms. We are also forced to consume an overwhelming amount of completely different content within a matter of seconds, in a way that our brains simply cannot fully process. And especially now, it feels more intense than ever. Instagram has also pushed us to limit ourselves creatively, stopping artists from experimenting with their images because of censorship, changing the crops and formats of our work to fit a standard, and making us feel that we should be doing what everyone else is doing simply because it worked for them and the brands they might be working for. We need healthier options so we stop destroying our mental health.

Three places you’ve felt inspired by.

Anywhere with good natural light coming through, anywhere with a sunset, and anywhere with interesting interiors.

What do you listen to on repeat?

Right now, “Uno” by Ben Yart.

What are the most worthwhile investments you've made?

Good accountants, a cheaper but better living space even if it’s further away from the city centre, and an emotionally stable partner.

What is an unusual habit, or an absurd thing, that you love?

I watch a lot of YouTube videos of doctors giving medical exams, people inspecting rooms, and airport pat-downs. They give me ASMR.

Tell us more about your creative process.

For me, something that is very inspiring is always my surroundings, especially how the light might affect certain surfaces in them. That’s why, when I think about a shoot, I immediately think about the location and what it could give us that could benefit artistically. And then I go from there.

Who is your forever inspo?

Sonia Szostak. She is a great photographer. She really knows how to blend in any situation and always creates something interesting.

Write us a fortune cookie.

Try to live any experience as positively as possible because almost everything is surmountable. With the right support and vibes, you will do it. Also, life is too short.

entry.content:
A visual inspiration platform for creatives — save, organize, search, and discover images, links, videos, articles, and text in a distraction-free, ad-free environment.

Sasha Gordon's Hard Candies (2026) is a portrait of a green woman admiring a translucent paperweight. Gordon builds her paintings from thin, translucent layers of oil, so the skin glows. She graduated from RISD in 2020. Her work is now in The Broad’s collection, and David Zwirner began co-representing her in 2024. Hard Candies hangs in Nocturnal at Zwirner Hong Kong through November 14.

Gordon often paints herself, using her body as what Zwirner calls "a kind of unorthodox avatar." Hard Candies is a rare exception: the sitter is someone else, peering into a crystal paperweight that belonged to Gordon's grandmother: a glass egg holding a tiny garden of red caps, orange toadstools, and a teal flower. It's an object inside a painting about loving an object.

Look closely, and she's doing exactly what you're doing right now.

entry.title: Turning the page
entry.summary: Books are on the runway, on your bag, and arranged by color. Reading them is optional.
entry.content:
Books are on the runway, on your bag, and arranged by color. Reading them is optional.

Now more than ever, books are props. Last year, the internet couldn't stop arguing about "performative reading" on the subway and at the bar, as if doomscrolling were better. Coach and Penguin Random House turned real books into bag charms. Alix Earle told Interview she’d never read a book, then offered “maybe Dr. Seuss.” The internet didn’t like that. Apparently, there’s a wrong way not to read, too.

In a 2025 Gallup survey, 43% of Gen Z students said they rarely or never read for fun.

Yes, the book is having a great year, even if no one's reading it.

entry.summary: A visual inspiration platform for creatives — save, organize, search, and discover images, links, videos, articles, and text in a distraction-free, ad-free environment.
entry.content:
A visual inspiration platform for creatives — save, organize, search, and discover images, links, videos, articles, and text in a distraction-free, ad-free environment.

Polina Osipova's Sliding towards the ancient (2026) is a pink felt rocket ship with a playground slide coming out of it. Osipova is a self-taught artist from the Indigenous Chuvash people of central Russia. Her pearl headpieces and silver coin headdresses went viral before she turned 25. She’s since had solo shows in London, New York, and now Berlin, where this piece lives at Neun Kelche. Her sculptures often use old family photos. Here, they're covered in thin metal plates, the way Orthodox icons are.

In Chuvash belief, people become stars when they die. Soviet playgrounds taught kids that space was something to conquer. Osipova's rocket heads the other way, toward the ancestors. Down the slide, it reads: "Voyage towards the ancient, I take my place in the sun." And yes, you're allowed to ride it.

entry.title: Shipwrecked
entry.summary: A castaway in 1866 sewed her own sealskin outfit to survive. 160 years later, Chanel is selling the look.
entry.content:
A castaway in 1866 sewed her own sealskin outfit to survive. 160 years later, Chanel is selling the look.

Ask anyone how they’re doing, and you’ll likely hear some version of “just trying to stay afloat” or “barely keeping my head above water.” It’s no wonder we’re all dressing like we just survived a shipwreck.

In 1866, Mary Ann Jewell was stranded in the sub-Antarctic after her ship went down. For 18 months, she survived in clothes she sewed from sealskin using needles carved from albatross bone.

Her ship sank with a fortune in gold aboard. But Mary Ann returned with something that earned her an unexpected payday. Now Chanel is selling her shipwreck aesthetic 160 years later.

entry.title: Iridescent Bowl
entry.summary: A visual inspiration platform for creatives — save, organize, search, and discover images, links, videos, articles, and text in a distraction-free, ad-free environment.
entry.content:
A visual inspiration platform for creatives — save, organize, search, and discover images, links, videos, articles, and text in a distraction-free, ad-free environment.

Katherine Gray’s shallow glass bowl runs from lavender to teal to sapphire to near-black, and the colors move when you do. Sandblasted to a fine, sandy matte, it’s coated in microscopically thin layers of metallic oxide and vaporized quartz — a NASA process Gray borrowed to shrink a James Turrell light field down to something you can cup in two hands.

Gray knows glass. A Canadian who took her MFA at RISD, she teaches glass at Cal State San Bernardino and judges Netflix’s Blown Away, and her work is in the Corning Museum of Glass. She knows the material well enough to make it do anything. Here, the bowl is flushed and poreless and warm to the eye. The color never quite settles anywhere you can point to. Tilt it, and the blue has already moved on.

entry.content:
A visual inspiration platform for creatives — save, organize, search, and discover images, links, videos, articles, and text in a distraction-free, ad-free environment.

Joyce Lin's table and chair are antiquities sealed away. Each block of matte blue acrylic suspends a blurred antique just out of reach. Lin is a Houston-based artist and furniture maker who treats familiar forms like chairs and tables as studies in dissection and mimicry. She studied furniture design at RISD and geology-biology at Brown; for this 2019 exhibition, she collaborated with Emeric Tchatchoua of the fashion label 3.Paradis on a series about dreams and remembrance.

The series was called “For Now We See Through A Glass Darkly,” which comes from 1 Corinthians 13:12 — a biblical banger about trying and failing to see what the future holds. Here, Lin looks back. The chair is a tufted comfort, evoking a weekend at Grandma’s. But it’s completely off-limits and forever out of reach.
